item.title: Limtiaco, Moylan outline differing approaches in congressional debate

item.content:encoded:
Alicia Limtiaco and Del. James Moylan outlined their priorities for Guam during a Guam Chamber of Commerce congressional debate ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.

Both candidates said Guam needs relief from high living costs, better access to federal funding and benefits, stronger infrastructure, and more economic opportunities. Both candidates also supported addressing the Jones Act’s impact on Guam’s shipping costs, expanding air service and competition, improving access to federal benefits, and returning unused federal land for local use. However, they offered different approaches to addressing those concerns.

Limtiaco, a former Guam attorney general and U.S. attorney, said her campaign would focus on fairness for Guam in federal programs, accountability for government spending, and creating more opportunities for local businesses and workers.

Limtiaco said she would push for more affordable housing by helping restore vacant or deteriorating homes through existing federal housing programs. To improve accountability, Limtiaco proposed tracking federal funding and project progress through public updates, as well as using congressional hearings and oversight to address delays or misuse of funds.

“I will establish a Guam Business and Economic Advisory Council to bring your experience into our congressional office, and I will report back on what has moved, what funding has been approved, and where work remains,” Limtiaco said.

Moylan emphasized his record in Congress and the federal funding and legislation he said he has helped secure for Guam. He said he would continue working to reduce barriers for local businesses, expand workforce opportunities, and pursue changes to shipping and air travel policies.

“These are real investments in the safety and well-being of our people, and I welcome the scrutiny,” Moylan said. “My commitment to serving you began long before this election. I served through the pandemic, through the devastation of Typhoon Mawar, and challenges that followed. Public service is a responsibility.”

On shipping, Moylan said he has introduced measures seeking exemptions from the Jones Act for Guam, including for fuel and emergencies. He said he would continue pushing a permanent exemption, while Limtiaco called for a broader review of how the law affects Guam and what changes would best address the island’s needs.

“I have already introduced with Congressman Ed Case from Hawaii over 11 measures that address the Jones Act exception specifically for Guam regarding fuel, regarding emergency situations,” Moylan said. “President Trump has extended the temporary Jones Act exception going on the seventh time. This is the opportunity where we can come together, people of quant, to present our argument even greater before Congress, before Senate, and get that permanent exception we need.”

Both candidates also support improving air connections to Guam and expanding tourism. Moylan highlighted his proposed Pacific Island Flight Alternatives Act, which he said would allow airlines from countries such as Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines to bring visitors to the Marianas and connect them to the U.S. mainland. He also supports a visa-waiver program for visitors from the Philippines.

Limtiaco said she would work with federal agencies, airlines, and industry representatives to find ways to improve air services and address policies that limit competition. She also identified the Philippines as a priority market for a visa-waiver program, citing potential benefits for tourism and the workforce.

The candidates agreed that Guam should receive better access to federal benefits, including Supplemental Security Income and improved Medicaid funding.

Moylan said he would continue pushing legislation to extend SSI to Guam and address limits on federal Medicaid funding. Limtiaco also supports SSI eligibility for Guam residents and removing Guam’s Medicaid funding cap. She said that, if the cap cannot be removed, she would seek adjustments that better reflect the cost of medical care and the number of people needing services.

On the military buildup, Limtiaco said Guam’s civilian community should benefit from federal investments and have a clearer picture of how funding is being spent and when projects will be completed. She identified the power grid, water system, roads, housing, education, and public services as areas needing attention.

Moylan pointed to federal military construction funding and community projects he said he has helped secure, including funding for roads, emergency facilities, and public safety vehicles. He argued that investments supporting infrastructure and pubic services outside military installations also benefit Guam residents.

In their discussion on jobs and workforce needs, Limtiaco identified ship repair as an area that could help diversify Guam’s economy, create jobs, and provide opportunities beyond the military buildup.

Moylan highlighted efforts to extend the H-2B temporary worker program through 2035 and support workforce training. He also pointed to legislation intended to reduce college tuition costs for students in U.S. territories, which he said had passed the House and was awaiting Senate action.

Both candidates said unused federal land should be returned for local use.

In her closing statement, Limtiaco said she would focus on fair treatment in federal programs, stronger infrastructure, and creating more opportunities for Guam’s residents and businesses.

Moylan closed by emphasizing experience, reliability, and following through on commitments. He said he has secured federal investments for Guam but acknowledged that more work remains.

The general election is scheduled for Tuesday.

item.title: CNMI voters head to polls early; runoff plans already underway

item.content:encoded:
A steady stream of voters lined up Tuesday at the Multi-Purpose Center on Saipan as early voting for the 2026 CNMI general election got underway across the Commonwealth, kicking off a seven-day advance voting period ahead of the Nov. 3 election.

Early voting is being conducted on Saipan, Tinian and Rota, giving voters an opportunity to cast ballots before Election Day. On Saipan, voting is taking place at the Multi-Purpose Center, while Tinian voters may vote at the Tinian Youth Center and Rota voters at Northern Marianas College Room B-2.

Commonwealth Election Commission Executive Director Kayla Igitol Magofna said election officials are prepared for what is expected to be a busy election season and are also developing contingency plans should any race require a runoff election.

"Yes, still we're doing that," Magofna said when asked whether the commission is preparing for a possible runoff.

Under Commonwealth law, a runoff election may be required if no candidate secures the vote threshold necessary for an outright victory. Election officials say the possibility remains particularly significant in the gubernatorial and attorney general races.

The gubernatorial contest featured former Gov. Ralph Torres and running mate Benjamin Jones Jr. against independent tickets headed by Rep. Jonathan "BJ" Attao and House Speaker Edmund Villagomez, as well as former Education Commissioner Lawrence Camacho and former Senate President Edith Deleon Guerrero.

Meanwhile, attorneys Joaquin "Jack" Torres, Jonathan "Robbie" Glass and Michael Evangelista are competing in the attorney general race, which will determine only the second elected attorney general in CNMI history.

Magofna said ballots cast during the general election will be tabulated using voting machines. If a runoff becomes necessary, however, election officials may hand-count ballots because runoff ballots likely would be printed locally.

"The hand counting, we probably will do that during the runoff because we're probably going to print runoff ballots on the island," she said.

Election officials are also reminding voters to bring valid identification, complete the required early-voting application and carefully review both sides of their ballots before casting them.

As of Sept. 19, the Commonwealth had 18,521 registered voters eligible to participate in the election.

Key election dates include the early voting period from Oct. 27 through Nov. 2 and General Election Day on Nov. 3. A runoff election will be scheduled following certification of results if required under Commonwealth election law.

item.title: CPUC to decide Thursday on Eastern Power solar project
item.description: The Commonwealth Public Utilities Commission is expected to decide Thursday whether to approve Eastern Power Solutions' proposed multimillion-dollar solar and battery storage project after completing a final review of the agreement and public feedback. item.content:encoded:
The Commonwealth Public Utilities Commission is expected to decide Thursday whether to approve Eastern Power Solutions' proposed multimillion-dollar solar and battery storage project after completing a final review of the agreement and public feedback.

Acting Chairman Bruce Camacho said commissioners are conducting one last review of the power purchase agreement and have been evaluating roughly 50 written comments submitted by members of the public.

"The Commission is conducting one final review of the contract and power purchase agreement," Camacho said. "Commissioners have also been sharing the written public comments received individually, and we are carefully reviewing approximately 50 submissions received thus far."

The anticipated decision comes as Eastern Power Solutions has warned that it could withdraw its proposal if regulators fail to act before Oct. 31, citing time-sensitive federal financing incentives tied to the project.

Camacho said the commission has also received a letter from Gov. David Apatang urging regulators to expedite their review. He said the governor reiterated his support for the project during a recent conversation.

"We acknowledge receipt of Gov. Apatang's letter urging the Commission to expedite its review," Camacho said. "I informed him that the Commission intends to convene at the earliest opportunity, Thursday, Oct. 29, to render a decision."

The governor and project supporters have argued that delays could jeopardize financing opportunities and federal tax credits viewed as critical to the project's success.

Among the public comments reviewed by commissioners were concerns about environmental and historic preservation issues. One commenter referenced controversy surrounding Guam's Mangilao solar farm and impacts on Marbo Cave.

Camacho said those concerns are being taken seriously but expressed confidence in the environmental review process.

"These concerns deserve serious consideration, particularly given the scale and long-term nature of the proposed project," he said.

Camacho added that revisions addressing liability and litigation concerns have clarified legal responsibilities between the parties involved. He also noted that any required environmental reviews, consultations and permits must be completed before project activities proceed.

While emphasizing that protecting ratepayers remains the commission's primary responsibility, Camacho said regulators recognize the potential benefits of renewable energy.

"I want to emphasize that the Commission is not attempting to delay this project unnecessarily," he said. "We recognize the potential benefits of renewable energy, including reducing our dependence on imported fossil fuels and providing greater long-term energy price stability for the people of Saipan, Tinian and Rota."

At the same time, Camacho said the proposed agreement represents a significant long-term commitment.

"However, this is a 25-year contractual commitment, and the Commission has a statutory responsibility to ensure that its decision is informed, legally sound and in the best interests of the Commonwealth," he said.

The commission is expected to announce its decision this Thursday.

item.content:encoded:
BILLINGS, Mont. — President Donald Trump said Tuesday that his administration is "terminating" a Biden-era rule that aimed to cut planet-warming emissions of methane from oil and gas drilling.

Trump said during a campaign rally in Texas that the change would save companies and consumers billions of dollars and unlock 210 million barrels of oil. That's equivalent to about 10 days of U.S. petroleum consumption.

The move aims to encourage more domestic drilling as Trump faces criticism over high fuel prices amid the war in Iran.

Methane is responsible for about a third of planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions, scientists estimate.

Cuts in methane emissions have emerged in recent years as a global priority to slow the rate of climate change. Oil and gas operations are the largest industrial source of methane, which is the main component in natural gas and far more potent to the atmosphere than carbon dioxide in the short term.

The invisible gas leaks from equipment and is released into the atmosphere or burned off as a waste product by oil drillers.

Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin previewed the changes last month, saying they would eliminate the agency's "Super Emitter Program" that requires companies to investigate and repair major methane releases from oil and natural gas facilities. The agency would also set less restrictive standards for small oil and gas wells.

Trump said during Tuesday's rally in Lubbock for Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton that Biden's plan "crushed the small operators" with crippling regulations.

"I'm officially terminating Biden's expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers $45 billion in costs," Trump said.

The loosening of the emissions rule comes as Trump and Republicans in Congress have been methodically dismantling climate policies enacted under former President Joe Biden. That's included the revocation of a scientific finding that was central to U.S. action on greenhouse gas emissions, lower fuel economy standards for vehicles and a move to repeal emission restrictions for coal and natural gas power plants.

Environmental groups said the latest rollback will let companies continue polluting the atmosphere with gas that could be captured and provide energy to millions of households.

Environmental Defense Fund President Fred Krupp said it gives a "free pass" to companies at the expense of American consumers.

"EPA should be fighting this waste, not making it easier," he said.

Zeldin has said the methane rule would have cost $18 billion and was holding back the U.S. energy industry.

The Biden methane rule was announced by officials including former Vice President Kamala Harris during a 2023 U.N. climate conference in the United Arab Emirates.

Federal officials under Biden said it would prevent an estimated 58 million tons (52.6 million metric tonnes) of methane emissions by 2038 and reduce other pollutants that cause health problems.

By 2034, the rule was projected to yield $98 billion in benefits. That figure was derived by calculating the future "social costs" of greenhouse gas emissions on public health and the environment, an approach rejected by Trump's EPA.

While previous regulations focused only on new oil and gas wells in the U.S., the Biden rule regulated existing wells. Operators also would have needed to plug leaking methane from smaller wells that produce just 6% of the nation's oil and gas while accounting for up to half of all methane emissions from oil and gas fields.

The final rule was published in 2024. The EPA last year imposed an 18-month delay to give companies time to meet new inspection requirements and other provisions.

The rule was crafted to be coordinated with a methane fee, approved in the 2022 climate law. The fee program would have levied a "waste emissions charge" of as much as $1,500 per metric ton of methane on energy producers that exceed a certain level of methane emissions.

The fee marked the first time the U.S. government directly imposed a fee, or tax, on greenhouse gas emissions. Congress repealed it weeks after Trump took office.

Officials also tried to rein in methane from oil and gas under former President Barack Obama, but that effort was scaled back during Trump's first term.

item.title: Rays stun Brewers with 2-run rally in 12th inning and force World Series Game 5
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Jonny DeLuca and pinch-hitter Ben Williamson singled home runs in a stunning 12th-inning rally, and the Tampa Bay Rays staved off World Series elimination with a 4-3 win over the Milwaukee Brewers on Tuesday night that forced Game 5. item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Jonny DeLuca and pinch-hitter Ben Williamson singled home runs in a stunning 12th-inning rally, and the Tampa Bay Rays staved off World Series elimination with a 4-3 win over the Milwaukee Brewers on Tuesday night that forced Game 5.

Cooper Pratt hit a tiebreaking home run off Ian Seymour in the top of the 12th for his fourth hit of the game as Milwaukee neared a sweep and its first World Series title.

But the Rays, also seeking their first championship, rallied in the bottom half after a throwing error by third baseman Joey Ortiz on Junior Caminero's leadoff grounder against reliever Antonio Senzatela.

Liam Hicks singled off rookie left-hander Shane Drohan, who relieved in his first appearance since Oct. 15, and DeLuca's single to center drove in pinch-runner Cedric Mullins to tie the score at 3.

Chandler Simpson's single loaded the bases and Milwaukee employed a five-man infield with the infield in.

Williamson, who had been 1 for 15 in the postseason, batted for Victor Mesa Jr. and hit a chopper over first baseman Jake Bauers into right field.

"That was totally what I told him to do," Rays manager Kevin Cash said, drawing laughs.

"Pretty big swing. I've got to go back and recall everything that took place."

Tampa Bay became the fourth team in World Series history to avoid elimination with an extra-inning comeback, according to OptaSTATS. The first three all went on to win the championship (1912 Red Sox, 1986 Mets, 2011 Cardinals).

"We've got a lot of fight in us. We're never going to shy away," Simpson said. "We were going to keep fighting until the end — the last inning, the last out, the last play, the last pitch. We were going to keep fighting. That's what we did tonight."

Game 5 in the best-of-seven matchup is Wednesday night at Tropicana Field, with NL Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski scheduled to start for the Brewers. Cash said he hadn't decided on a starter yet.

Tampa Bay became just the fifth of 26 teams that fell behind 3-0 in the World Series to win Game 4. The previous four lost Game 5.

Of 43 teams to trail 3-0 in any best-of-seven postseason matchup, the only one that rebounded to win was the Boston Red Sox against the New York Yankees in the 2004 American League Championship Series.

"It just shows the resiliency of this group," Williamson said. "We continue to fight, and that's been the motto this series and this full season, is just fight."

Caminero was replaced by Mullins at third base and hobbled off the field with an ailing left foot. But the All-Star slugger said he'll definitely play Wednesday night.

"He'll play tomorrow on one leg. I'll make sure of it," Cash said.

Tampa Bay ended an eight-game winning streak by the Brewers, who were bidding to become only the second team to sweep a League Championship Series and the World Series.

"If you want to win a championship, you've got to survive some hard things," Milwaukee captain Christian Yelich said. "Like I said earlier, it's supposed to be hard. It's supposed to test you. We understand that."

David Hamilton also homered for the Brewers. Jackson Chourio had a single and double, improving to 10 for 20 in the Series.

Pratt, a 22-year-old rookie whose go-ahead hit sparked the Brewers to a 5-4 win in Game 2, drove a slider into the left-field seats against Seymour. Pratt had tied the score at 1 with an RBI double in the second.

Milwaukee players bounded out of the dugout to greet Pratt, who debuted in June and became the first rookie to hit an extra-inning homer in the World Series.

"This kid responds to everything," Brewers manager Pat Murphy said.

Seymour also allowed Frelick's tying homer in Game 2.

Milwaukee fans in the crowd of 40,514, many waving yellow towels and some wearing cheeseheads, brought a Badger State feel to Tropicana Field.

Tampa Bay returned to its white home jerseys, a day after playing in Devil Rays throwbacks.

Simpson hit an RBI double off starter Dustin May in the second, but Milwaukee tied the score in the fourth against Griffin Jax when Frelick hit a two-out single and came around on Pratt's double.

Caminero singled leading off the bottom half to chase May and advanced on a groundout. DeLuca hit a hard grounder to Hamilton and Caminero twisted toward the grass to avoid the third baseman's tag, then came home when Hamilton bounced his throw past Bauers for an error.

Hamilton, Milwaukee's No. 9 hitter, drove an 0-2 fastball at the letters from Jax into the right-field seats for his second home run of the postseason — half his regular-season total and just his second since June 6.

item.title: U.S. to issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro as his whereabouts remain unclear
item.description: RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil — The United States says it will issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and his family, amid multiple reports that the defeated Brazilian presidential candidate has left the country following Sunday's election. His whereabouts have not been independently confirmed. Bolsonaro, a conservative politician and ally of President Donald Trump, lost Sunday's presidential election to incumb
item.content:encoded:
RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil — The United States says it will issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and his family, amid multiple reports that the defeated Brazilian presidential candidate has left the country following Sunday's election. His whereabouts have not been independently confirmed.

Bolsonaro, a conservative politician and ally of President Donald Trump, lost Sunday's presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by more than four million votes, just three weeks after winning the first round. While Bolsonaro's Liberal Party has since recognized Lula's victory, Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat.

On Tuesday a senior U.S. administration official said that the State Department would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family, allowing them to enter the country.

The visa announcement comes as Bolsonaro faces multiple investigations in Brazil, including allegations of money laundering and tax evasion, which he denies. On Monday Brazil's Supreme Court ordered him to surrender his passports within 24 hours and barred him from leaving the country.

The order followed comments by Bolsonaro's brother Eduardo, who lives in self-imposed exile in Florida, suggesting Flávio should leave Brazil if he lost the election.

In a video released that day, Bolsonaro said federal police officers had stopped him outside the home of his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, and ordered him to surrender his passports. The former far-right leader is under house arrest after being sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup following his own defeat by Lula in the 2022 presidential election.

"I never thought about leaving the country," Flávio Bolsonaro said in the video. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this aberration." He described the order as an attempt to intimidate him.

On Tuesday, Brazilian media reported that Bolsonaro had left for the United States. His campaign manager, his lawyer and other political allies had earlier said they did not know his whereabouts.

Lula won the election with just over 51% of the valid votes, or approximately 64.2 million, compared with more than 48%, or nearly 59.8 million, for Bolsonaro.

President Trump has repeatedly cast doubt on Lula's victory, suggesting on Monday that the election was "rigged", without offering any evidence. He returned to the subject at a campaign rally in Texas on Tuesday night, as he accused Democrats of election fraud.

"Brazil is also doing a good job of it, aren't they? Did you see that? I didn't take sides, but it didn't look very good," he said.

Lula criticised Bolsonaro's reported departure during celebrations for his 81st birthday in Brasília on Tuesday.

"Those who have nothing to hide have nothing to fear," Lula told supporters.

"He could have stayed and proven that the accusations [against him] are not true," Lula said, adding that he regretted Bolsonaro's departure.

He also took aim at the Bolsonaro family's close ties to the Trump administration. "Brazil is their second home; their first home is the United States," he said.

item.title: Southwest flood damage estimates are hundreds of millions for New Mexico alone
item.description: Intense rainstorms linked to a very active El Niño-driven Pacific hurricane season have left thousands of people in the Four Corners states displaced or facing massive cleanups from flooding. item.content:encoded:
Intense rainstorms linked to a very active El Niño-driven Pacific hurricane season have left thousands of people in the Four Corners states displaced or facing massive cleanups from flooding.

The adjoining states of Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Arizona all saw substantial flooding last week, and damage assessments are just starting to trickle in from cities, towns and some of the most remote territory in the continental U.S.

The northern New Mexico city of Farmington was hit particularly hard after torrential rains fell on the San Juan mountains in Colorado, sending floodwaters down the San Juan River that passes through Farmington on its way to Lake Powell on the Utah-Arizona border.

Small towns all along the river, from Pagosa Springs, Colorado, to Bloomfield, New Mexico and Bluff, Utah all saw historic flooding and are now assessing recovery challenges.

About 46,000 people live in Farmington, long a center for coal, oil and natural gas production. It's also an important hub for the northeast side of the Navajo reservation, which sprawls across three states.

Farmington residents started getting evacuation notices on their phones as early as Wednesday night.

"My sister was notified on Thursday that she had to get out," said Connie Gooch, who has lived in Farmington for more than 65 years.

Gooch's sister owns a house in a suburban neighborhood near the San Juan River.

"Every year she goes through this," Gooch said. "The river starts rising, and she starts making sandbags to put around. But this year it was so fast she didn't have time to do that."

According to National Weather Service data from a river gauge in Farmington , the San Juan grew 13 times larger in just 36 hours, late last week.

In the wee hours of Thursday morning, the river was about 3.5 feet high. By Friday, it was 14 feet high, flooding neighborhoods across the city, and possibly setting a record for the highest water ever recorded in the city.

This even after the Navajo Reservoir upstream from Farmington was able to mostly contain water rushing down from the mountains. But downstream of the reservoir, flood surges into the city came from two normally dry tributaries, Gobernador Canyon and Cañon Largo.

"This is a catastrophic flood of historic proportions," said Devon Neeley, San Juan County's public information officer.

"This river got wider than we have ever seen it in our lifetimes."

Similar reports are coming in from the other side of the San Juan mountains in Colorado.

"It's nothing like most of us have seen before," said Tyler Schmidt, captain of the fire and rescue team in the small town of South Fork, Colo. on the banks of the Rio Grande. "We had several neighborhoods that were under two to three feet of water."

Colorado Public Radio's Dan Boyce reports that responders' immediate priorities are lifting final evacuation orders as waters recede. Damaged bridges need to be assessed. Well water all down the Rio Grande's path in the San Luis valley needs to be tested.

Other drinking water impacts from the storm include sewage spills from flooded treatment plants in Sedona, Arizona and other locations. KNAU reports extensive damage on the Hopi reservation.

The Hopi reservation is surrounded by the Navajo reservation, where there have also been reports of rescues, washed out roads and flooding of historic proportions.

San Juan County, New Mexico's Neeley said fire crews, police officers, National Guard troops, and even out-of-state swift water teams rescued between 200 and 300 county residents.

"We have pulled people out of vehicles stuck in running washes. We have pulled people by helicopter off of rooftops," Neeley said. "We have used not only high-clearance vehicles from the National Guard, but amphibious vehicles because the water is so high. It's been a lot."

By Sunday, the rain had eased, river levels were falling, and some residents started returning home to assess flood damage.

Connie Gooch delivered tarps and other materials to her sister's house.

"The river was up four feet in her house," she said.

She found a neighborhood full of people moving furniture out of their homes and piling demolition debris in their front yards.

"There were trucks and cars all over the place," Gooch said. "There was a guy in front of me carrying a loaded trailer full of sheet rock that they'd chipped out of somebody's house."

But officials want the thousands of evacuated residents to stay out for now.

"The public is anxious to get back in; we recognize that, we're sympathetic to that," said San Juan County Fire Chief David Vega at a public briefing Sunday. "Now that the swift water component is out of the way, that exposes a whole new set of hazards for us," Vega added.

Public officials are concerned about hazards like raw sewage and damaged gas lines, live power lines, and the floodwater itself.

"The water is not healthy," Vega said. "Stay out of the water. Gas, diesel, pesticides, fertilizer, these are not things that you want on your clothes."
